questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I have been to Germany many times and wanted to immerse myself in the culture while also becoming fluent in the language. I chose Munich specifically, because I found it more interesting than Heidelberg, and I had already been to Berlin many times. Also, the weather is different from the Danish weather with its warmth. In addition, I checked out the courses beforehand, and they seemed interesting. This didn't matter though, as the course catalogue was wildly different from what was offered the year before, and I wasn't able to see what was offered in my semester of Summer '22 beforehand.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The short answer is, I was thrilled to be in Munich learning about different cultures and meeting people from all over the world. I was though very disappointed in the University for multiple reasons. Most importantly, the course information was lacking or non-existent before my semester start so my academic experience was a bit of a patchwork of making the courses work for me. The practicalities of living in Germany were also a bit of a hassle. I recommend a more digitalized or less bureaucratic country than Germany, or both.
I also dealt with some personal difficulties back home, which made it hard for me to fully enjoy the exchange and influenced my overall experience.

A more thorough answer will be posted in the upcoming boxes.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
LMU provided me with an amazing PDF that basically answered all my questions regarding housing, transport, registering for courses and household stuff.
However, this PDF was not specifically made for mathematics, so much of the info was just "this is the default at LMU, but your faculty might do it differently". And the mathematics faculty often did...

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Which leads me to my second point, personal help for whenever I had questions that were not answered in the introductory PDF. The help desk was in the main LMU building, which was very convenient, except that it was closed due to the coronavirus. This meant I had to send e-mails to the exchange help team. They did reply quickly, but it would've been much better with personal, live assistance. I can't recall specifically what they helped me with.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Difficult, had it not been for the offer I received through LMU.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
It pays to write your application for renting an apartment in German. I have heard that the succes rates are much higher when you write in German than in English.
Germans value their peace and quiet, so be prepared to respect your neighbors' boundaries.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I was not very happy when I discovered only 30% of students were gonna be offered student housing in the lottery. It made me very nervous about the prospect of having to find housing in a different city. I did not win this lottery, but I was sent an offer to a private apartment. I said yes immediately and was quite satisfied with the place. Upsides were: fair rent, close to uni and city center, south-facing terrace. Downsides were: living alone (for me personally I felt lonely often and would rather have lived with roomies or in a dormitory), construction works in a neighboring block, poor sound insulation, poor cooling in the summer, and no wi-fi included. As I said, I think German people value their peace and quiet a lot, so it was difficult to be young and spontaneous. 
Overall, the upsides listed are quite rare in the Munich housing market, so I was grateful for the apartment, even if there were some downsides.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Upsides: The flexibility in registering for courses was amazing. I could sign up for an exam a week before the date of the exam. UCPH is more bureaucratic regarding signing up for (or dropping) a course. This flexibility was also quite appropriate, due to the downsides.

Downsides: I had to e-mail each professor that I wanted to take their course instead of just ticking a box in a form. Also, there was no information about the curriculum beforehand, which meant I had to take a course to find out if I wanted to take that course... I was recommended to come to all the lectures in the first week of all the courses I considered, and then decide. Some courses (seminars) had very few spots, which I wasn't informed of. I didn't manage to get a spot for those.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The process is that you either:
- Show up to classes and talk to the professor
- E-mail them
In some cases, seats were quite limited, so e-mailing the professor well beforehand was essential. This was often the "Seminar" classes, where each student would do a presentation, so you could only have x students if the semester had x lectures. 
Signing up was very flexible and could be done very close to the exam.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I suppose I could've gotten help from the exchange coordinator, but I didn't need it, so I don't know whether it was provided.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Of the 57 ECTS worth of courses I got pre-approved, only 21 ECTS were offered. Also, one of my desired courses was a Seminar, so it had too few seats when I tried to sign up for me to get one.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Advice: Do not expect that a course is offered just because it was offered previously. If you come to LMU for the courses, write e-mails to the professors as you are deciding which universities to apply to. That way you can get a sense of whether your desired courses will in fact be offered and hear about the curriculum.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I was dissatisfied about LMU for multiple reasons. First, the course catalogue website, called LSF, was confusing.
lsf.verwaltung.uni-muenchen.de
is the link if you want to have a look.
It was in my opinion poorly designed and there was virtually no information about any course. Only the course title, which was sometimes misleading. I planned to take Topology 2, which sounded like a good idea, as I had taken Topology in UCPH already. This course at LMU turned out to be Algebraic Topology 2, which was too hard, unless I read up on 9 ECTS worth of algebraic topology on my own. Also, as I said before, the info for a particular semester was uploaded late, so I had to check last year's corresponding semester. This meant that I intended to take some courses but ended up taking entirely different ones. Only 21 of my 57 ECTS points of pre-approved courses were actually offered. If I had known that the courses I would end up taking were wildly different from my intended courses, I honestly would have stayed home or gone to another German university. The only thing that gives LMU 2 stars is that the curriculum in MAML and HELA was well put together, that HELA was really interesting and that the lecturers were generally good at teaching. These abbreviations are explained in the "list of courses".
One of my lecturers was unfortunately not very keen to answer questions, which I had many of since I didn't have the correct prerequisites, since there was literally no info online. It was not very comfortable to come to his lectures in Topology 2, which is one of the reasons I dropped the course.
Lastly, the schedule system was ineffective. I assume there was basically no system for the professors to avoid having their classes simultaneously. At UCPH (SCIENCE) we have schedule blocks that do not overlap, so the student knows not to take two courses in the same schedule block. That is one way to solve the problem, and I am sure there are many others. I was taking 16 hours of teaching each week, but I was only able to show up to 10 of them, as the remaining 6 were at the same time as the 10.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of courses was, on average, similar to at UCPH. Some of it was harder and some of it was easier than at UCPH. I think Verdichtete Mathematik was mainly targeted toward PhD students, which was part of the reason I failed it.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Style of teaching: The style of teaching was very close to how it is at UCPH, but everything around the teaching was different. There was no single platform for courses and homework. I took three courses at three different professors. One used Uni2work, the other used Moodle, and the third uploaded files to his website on
lmu.de
.
Two of my three courses had no lecture notes. We were expected to come to class and write everything the lecturer did. This is very old-fashioned in my opinion.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Mathematical and Applications to Machine Learning (MAML, easier than at UCPH, maybe would have been BA level at UCPH)
Halbeinfache Lie-Algebren (HELA, comparable to UCPH)
Verdichtete Mathematik (VM, harder than UCPH, probably targeted toward PhD students). This course I failed.
I listed the difficulty to clarify what I wrote in "level of courses".

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend Halbeinfache Lie-Algebren. It is a course about the classification of all finite-dimensional complex semi-simple lie algebras. The curriculum is kind of big, but you prove some amazing results, and you aren't expected to remember everything at the (oral) exam. The course was offered for the first time in '22, and we weren't that many taking it, so maybe it won't be offered again...

questions.answer: I thought wi-fi would be included in the rent.

questions.answer: Beer was cheaper than I had thought 😉

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had a lot of opportunities to meet people through MESA, which is the Munich Erasmus Student Association. I found some good friends and spent a lot of time with them. However, I didn't use these opportunities that much, as I dealt with a lot of personal issues.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
As you can see here, MESA arranges many events, and they are all free or at least fairly priced.
https://mesa.esn-germany.de/events
There was for example nature trips (lakes, hikes, alps), karaoke night once a week, a city tour, a tour to Dachau, sightseeing, day-trips to other cities (Salzburg for example), trips to the English Garden.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Deutsches Museum. It is a huge museum about tech and science, both modern and historical. It takes maybe 3 full days to see everything, or 1-2 if you're not interested in literally everything. In general the Munich museums are interesting, cheap (most are cheaper on sundays) and there are many of them. But I recommend the Deutsches Museum the most.
The English Garden is a wonderful place to hang out or tan or take a run or have a beer. It's huge.
Olympiadorf is also great for the same things, and there is a Bierstube for students with very cheap beer and food.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Erdinger Therme is a huge spa with everything from sauna and massage to waterslides. It is not cheap, but it is relaxing and comforting. And you can buy drinks in the pool. And go to the Alps. I went to Eibsee a few times and took the lift to Zugspitze. The lift is kind of expensive, but it is the highest point in Germany after all. And swimming in an Alp lake is wonderful and free, after you've payed for transport. 
Visit a brewery. It's not expensive if you go a few people, it is good fun and you get to try different kinds of freshly brewed beer on tap. I recommend Ayinger, as it is more intimate and not so heavily visited.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
I honestly thought Munich would be closer to Copenhagen culturally. I somehow found Münchners more closed than Copenhageners. Germans very much appreciate peace and quiet, so living in an apartment complex with thin walls was tough. There was a note on the wall warning that legal steps would be taken if I made extensive noise after 22. This was durable for a semester, but it was not comfortable for me personally.
And the bike culture is nothing like in Denmark (more information on that in the "challenging" section). I thought it was easy to get used to the party vibe though. Munich had so many big events over the course of my semester like concerts, (student) festivals, museum exhibitions, art shows, sport events and demonstrations. I wasn't bothered by how these events sometimes got in the way of traffic and my route through the city. I just thought it was cool to have so many things going on.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Learn German. I think everyone's personality is more "their true selves" when they speak in their native tongue. So you can get to know local students better if you speak German with them.
Try talking to people from your classes who look approachable. I didn't really get German friends, because I was too scared to talk to people in my classes. But I would've liked to do that more.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Traffic was challenging. When I was biking, I was almost run over by right-swinging cars about 10 times during my stay. Pedestrians often walk on the bike path like it's the most natural thing in the world. And many people on bikes were on the left side of the road whenever it is more convenient for them. I know this happens in Copenhagen too, but way more often in Munich in my opinion. Lastly, the bike infrastructure was messy and traffic lights were often shared with pedestrians, making it less efficient to get around.

At uni, there were quite few events for the math institute compared to UCPH. More events would have allowed me to get to know more local math students which I desired, but that could be due to the coronavirus.

German digitalization is behind the Danish, and their (in my opinion high level of) bureaucracy can be frustrating. This means you have to call or send letters if you want customer service. This was hard to adjust to, but luckily their postal service is faster and cheaper than the Danish/Nordic one, Post Nord.

Sometimes my friends would suggest going to a restaurant where I had to eat at home because they had nothing vegan except for potatoes and salad. As a vegan, this was a bit rough.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
I liked how Municians have traditions and aren't afraid of sticking to them. This sometimes caused problems like finding vegan food (as per above), but generally I liked it.
 
I also liked that Munich have a habit of going out for drinks and food often. The sidewalk was full of life from the center of the city and pretty far out, since there was always a restaurant in sight with people talking (outside in the summer, which is extra cozy). They had many different types of world cuisines, which I enjoyed exploring. I can recommend Orange Box, Charlie's Vegan, Soy Vegan, Tahdig, Emmi's, Siggis and Schwabinger Osterwaldgarten. As I am vegan, I can't tell you much about traditional Bavarian food except Schwabinger Osterwaldgarten, which my friends and family thought had great traditional dishes.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
-Be prepared to send a lot of e-mails to professors if you actually want to know about the content of your courses before you take the courses. 
-Learn German. It is useful for socializing, some courses are only offered in German, and a lot of customer service is either better in German or only offered in German.
-Plan your time well. I wasted a lot of afternoons doing nothing because I had nothing planned and I was done studying for the day. There is so much to do in and around Munich, so be sure to try these things when you're not studying.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
The Erasmus+ grant dates, for how long your stay is going to be, are only able to be corrected to fewer days than your initial estimate, not more days. This means you might end up getting a smaller grant than you are entitled to.
Therefore, when you apply for the grant be sure to write more days than you expect to be abroad. You can't know about your exam dates beforehand, so write the end date as if your last exam is very late. You can always correct it once you find out more.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
I am now much better at dealing with troublesome authorities, companies and institutions. By that I mean sending e-mails sooner rather than later and calling them to ask questions. I am less nervous talking about something serious in a language I don't command fully. 
I understand my personality and culture much better in relation to others. Many times in Munich I thought other people were weird, but that's just because they are from different countries and cultures. I thought the whole world's idea of a "normal person" was like the Danes' idea of a "normal person", but it's not. This ties in with how I learned a lot about how different our cultures are across the world. I thought biking culture sucked, an American friend of mine thought it was great! I thought the Münchners liked to dance and party a lot, a Brazilian friend thought they liked it... not so much. It was a big eye opener for me, and I look forward to travelling to different places later in life.
My German improved a lot and I learned to fit into a different University system. I learned how to socialize with strangers and find things to talk about even if we had different interests.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
The university of LMU was my biggest challenge during my exchange. As explained above, it was troublesome in many ways, and it removed the focus from the curriculum.
This, combined with my personal difficulties in Denmark, meant that my mental health was not so good for the majority of my stay. I was conflicted between giving up and moving back home and trying to "brush it off" and just keep working and enjoying my stay. I ended up doing a mix, visiting Denmark a few times.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I think finding a balance between studying, socializing, sightseeing, and taking care of my mental health was the biggest reason my exchange was, in my opinion, unsuccessful. This was triggered mainly by the difficulties at LMU. If you have an academic reason to go to LMU (a specific course you're crazy about or a professor you're eager to do a project with), you should definitely study at LMU. If you're going on exchange for the cultural and social aspects, I would recommend another university.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
